articles.title: Political polarization and press freedom in Africa: a scoping review (of research literature)
articles.authors: Samuel Danso, Theodora Dame Adjin-Tettey, Martin Thompson Kwadzo Ntem
articles.abstract: Political and media polarization tend to perpetuate divisions and audience perceptions of bias, leading to social unrest and the undermining of consensus-building. This scoping review provides an overview of empirical studies on polarization and press freedom between 2014 and 2024 to ascertain the nature of research, thematic areas covered, and gaps that could inform future research. Aided by Arksey and O’Malley’s methodological framework, 28 articles retrieved from four prominent journalism and media studies databases and publishing outlets that met the inclusion criteria of the study were thematically analyzed. The findings show limited publications of articles in African-based journals compared to their Western counterparts. Ethiopia emerged as a focal point for most of the studies on polarization and press freedom, particularly along ethnic divides. The study identified thematic areas covered to include assessment of the media environment, media polarization and political participation through the media, interrogation of Western conceptualizations and theoretical lenses for understanding media polarization and proposals for African-centered ones, journalists and civil society’s role in holding political actors accountable in polarized environments, and journalists’ professional challenges in polarized media contexts. The study recommends, among others, that future studies further interrogate African-centered conceptualizations around media polarization.

articles.title: Nostalgia bait and the political economy of time: Future shock in algorithmic culture
articles.abstract: This study examines how platform capitalism transforms temporal distress into economic value through “nostalgia bait”—algorithmically optimized content that remediates recent cultural artefacts to extract engagement from users experiencing technological acceleration. Integrating Toffler's (1970) concept of future shock with Sharma's (2014) power-chronography, the research demonstrates how platforms incorporate the psychological conditions they claim to address, converting temporal anxiety into a core profit mechanism. Using dual methods—thematic analysis of 5610 TikTok comments and semi-structured interviews with ten music industry professionals—the study traces recursive relationships between user temporal displacement and creator labor constraints. Findings reveal three dynamics of temporal exploitation: (1) platforms commodify psychological responses to acceleration through manufactured nostalgia, with 42% of comments expressing temporal displacement; (2) algorithmic systems restructure creative labor through recommendation dependencies, compelling producers to optimize content around seven-second attention windows and content calendar logic rather than artistic vision; (3) embodied nostalgic affect becomes extractable behavioral data through the standardization of sensory language, including phrases such as “unexplainable chills” and “core memory.” The research advances three theoretical contributions: extending future shock theory to demonstrate how conditions identified in 1970 become engineered features of 21st-century business models; operationalizing power-chronography through empirical analysis of platform temporal architectures; and systematically connecting production and consumption dynamics to reveal self-reinforcing cycles of extraction. The findings carry implications for temporal sovereignty in algorithmic culture and for the development of alternative infrastructures oriented toward human continuity rather than platform profit.

articles.title: Queer from the start: The utopianism of LGBTQ+ NFT collectors
articles.abstract: While much has been written about the volatility of digital assets, academic scholarship has largely overlooked how blockchain technologies have been adopted and reimagined by LGBTQ+ communities. This article addresses that gap through a digital ethnography of queer NFT communities active during the crypto craze of 2022, combining online participant observation with semi-structured interviews. Drawing on José Esteban Muñoz’s concept of queer futurity, it examines how queer users imagined blockchain as a speculative platform for alternative economic and social possibility—despite the financial risks embedded in the technology’s libertarian and capitalist structures. The article interrogates the utopian rhetoric of inclusion, decentralisation, and wealth redistribution that was deployed within these communities to justify their interest in and holdings of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) and cryptocurrency. Queer leaders leveraged the blockchain to foster inclusive digital communities and promote wealth circulation amongst LGBTQ+ individuals, while community members embraced the technology as a risky opportunity for queer economic mobility. The article positions blockchain as a contested site where competing futurities collide—offering the illusion of liberation and the reproduction of existing inequalities. It argues that while queer users sought to make the blockchain ‘queer from the start,’ their efforts were ultimately constrained by the capitalist logics that underpin the technology.

articles.title: In their own words: A mixed-methods analysis of Iranian fansubbers’ motivations and perceptions
articles.abstract: Due to Iran’s strict censorship regulations, fansubbing has allowed Iranians to bypass these restrictions and access a wider range of media. Grounded in the theoretical framework of cybersubtitling and non-professional translation, my paper situates fansubbing as a distinct socio-cultural practice driven by intrinsic, non-commercial motivations that operate in parallel to the state-sanctioned industry. Although the reception has received attention, it is unclear empirically why Iranian fansubbers produce subtitles and what their comments and perceptions are. Therefore, my mixed-methods study identifies the main categories of motivations, reasons, and perceptions for doing such activity among them. The results indicated that there was a strong focus on providing free fansubs to users, and the reasons included religious beliefs, altruism, and opposition to charges for translation. The results also revealed that participants believe the perceived low quality of current professional subtitling and dubbing in Iran can be attributed to a lack of respect and recognition for the translators. Additionally, fansubbers felt that the translators selected for professional translations were not solely evaluated based on their qualifications, leading to the new phenomenon of professional subtitlers plagiarizing from fansubs. This highlights a paradox where the “amateur” field of cybersubtitling upholds quality standards often neglected by the professional sector.

articles.title: Breaking through barriers and shadowbans: How disabled influ-activists navigate algorithmic challenges
articles.abstract: Despite disability’s centrality to digital inclusion debates, scholarship on disabled influencers remains limited, focusing primarily on representation rather than material advocacy conditions. This study examines how disabled influencers navigate platform constraints while pursuing digital advocacy, extending Van Dijk’s access framework to content creation contexts through semi-structured interviews with sixteen Italian content creators on Instagram and TikTok. Digital inclusion emerges not as linear progression but as ongoing negotiation with systematically biased technological and commercial systems. Findings reveal sophisticated adaptive strategies including “algorithmic advocacy literacy” and “experiential pedagogy” that transform lived experience into educational resources. However, these operate within structural constraints including “systematic advocacy suppression” through shadowbanning, automated content removal, and monetization restrictions. The study introduces “accessibility maintenance work,” invisible, uncompensated labour creators perform to make platforms genuinely accessible, while revealing economic stratification where resource availability directly correlates with advocacy capacity. Results challenge approaches privileging technological solutions over systematic reform, demonstrating how platform governance constrains advocacy through accumulated algorithmic bias and automated moderation lacking contextual understanding.

articles.title: Awe, Attention, and the Psychology of Perception
Public Self-Consciousness and Anticipatory Avatar Customization in Korean Metaverse Platform
articles.authors: Upyong Hong, Hyenyeong Chung, Yunju Nam
articles.abstract: This study examines how public self-consciousness influences anticipatory avatar customization in Korean metaverse platform environments. In Study 1, 50 Korean university students created avatars under four conditions using iFland: free creation, private context, public context, and actual-self representation. Study 2 involved 100 independent raters evaluating the public suitability of freely created avatars. Results revealed that 96 percent created avatars differing from their actual appearance. Counterintuitively, individuals with higher public self-consciousness and agreeableness were significantly less likely to modify avatars for public contexts ( p < 0.05). Study 2 confirmed that unmodified avatars were rated more suitable for public contexts ( p < 0.05), suggesting that socially conscious individuals proactively incorporated appropriateness into initial designs. These preliminary findings suggest that Korean university students’ cultural emphasis on social harmony may shape virtual identity through anticipatory rather than reactive customization, though cross-cultural replication with diverse samples is needed to establish the generalizability of these patterns.

articles.title: The Perfect Match: How Artificial Intelligence Is Industrializing Romance Fraud
Online Social Anxiety in the Digital Age: Transitions, Predictors, and Mental Health Associations in Emerging Adulthood
articles.authors: Ao Liu, Zheng Zhang, Xintian Hong, Rumiao Pan, Zhihao Ma, Yuanyuan Wang
articles.abstract: Background: Online social anxiety (OSA), a multidimensional form of social evaluative anxiety in online social contexts, disproportionately affects emerging adults who constitute the largest active group of media users and face heightened psychological sensitivity due to growing pressures and immature sociocognitive regulation during the transition to adulthood. However, its heterogeneity, transitions, and longitudinal associations with mental health outcomes remain underexplored. Methods: This study utilized data from two waves of a three-wave longitudinal survey, with 849 Chinese participants ( Mean age = 21.6 years; 50.4 percent female) assessed at 4-month intervals. Individuals were classified using latent profile analysis and the stability and changes of profiles were assessed via latent transition analysis (LTA). Multinomial logistic regressions were conducted separately at baseline and follow-up to identify correlates of profile membership. Predictors of profile transitions were examined using manual three-step LTA models, and associations between latent transition patterns and follow-up mental health outcomes were examined using BCH-LTA distal outcome analyses controlling for the corresponding baseline symptom level. Results: Four profiles of OSA were identified: low, privacy-sensitive, moderate-high, and high OSA. Extreme profiles (low/high OSA) showed high stability (80.4 percent and 79.1 percent), while privacy-sensitive OSA exhibited the lowest stability (55.1 percent). Profile memberships were influenced by social-cognitive biases and digital interaction, particularly fear of negative evaluation and online interpersonal trust, whereas profile transitions were mainly associated with anxiety. Transitions toward less severe OSA profiles were generally associated with better subsequent mental health, whereas transitions toward more severe profiles corresponded to poorer outcomes, particularly for offline social anxiety. Conclusion: OSA was heterogeneous in its manifestation, severity and transitions. Personalized and early interventions targeting profile-specific vulnerabilities are critical to prevent the worsening of OSA and mitigate its psychological burden.

articles.title: Trust beyond algorithms: What drives Italian audiences’ perceptions of search results and news produced with AI
articles.abstract: This article examines what drives audiences’ trust levels across different configurations of artificial intelligence (AI) use within the information ecosystem. We rely on a representative survey of Italian adults, performed in September 2025, to analyse trust patterns when (a) AI acts as an intermediary through automated search results and (b) when it is embedded in news organisations. Our findings show that AI-generated search results are more trusted than news, highlighting the growing role of platforms as primary information providers. Moreover, trust in news is positively associated with trust in news produced with AI, regardless of the source, challenging prevailing assumptions of ‘algorithmic aversion’ even in a traditional setting like Italy. These results suggest a shift in the foundations of media trust, with important implications for the role of journalism in an increasingly platform-driven information ecosystem.

articles.title: Working with coding communication: the digital reframing of work-related meaning processing systems examined from a Luhmannian perspective
articles.abstract: Purpose From a conceptual perspective based on Luhmann's social systems theory, we examine how digital technologies – notably those of artificial intelligence (AI) – can reframe work-related meaning processing from which workers and organizations perceive work meaningfulness. Design/methodology/approach From a Luhmannian perspective, this research first advances a conceptual framework that considers (1) work as communication that can belong to a series of communication systems and that organizes structural couplings between these systems at the individual, organizational and societal levels and (2) digital technologies as mediums that intermediate work-related communication systems and codify work-related structural couplings. It next connects the framework with the empirical issues identified from an exploratory analysis of 137 existing studies to elucidate how digital mediums can reframe work in terms of meaning processing for workers as well as for organizations. Findings Our analysis stipulates that (1) digital mediums, doubly intermediating work-related meaning processing notably between workers and organizations, draw on and, in parallel, engender codifying references that normalize, formalize, signify and interconnect work-related communication and structure couplings; (2) the amplification of codifying references could stimulate self-referencing processes by forming coding communication technical systems that reframe different work-related meaning processing systems, which include psychic systems (e.g. workers) and social systems (e.g. organizations) and (3) the structural intermediateness afforded by digital mediums between these systems could affect the ways in which work meaningfulness is individually, organizationally and societally perceived. Originality/value This research provides a conceptual prism based on Luhmann's social systems theory to address the timely preoccupation related to the implications of AI for work. Its contributions can be mobilized, for example, to study from a systemic view (1) how to understand digitally reframed work and work meaningfulness, (2) how to specify and, if necessary, converge digitally meaningful work, psychically meaningful work and societally meaningful work, (3) how to preserve workers' meaning processing in the context of working with AI and (4) how to capture the societal effects of working with coding communication by considering the interconnection between multilevel work-related systems.

articles.title: Determinants of pre-interaction swift trust and long-term adoption of care robots: the role of mind attribution and perceived similarity in eldercare robotics
articles.authors: Mahed Maddah, Shirin Hasavari, Shadi Esnaashari, Pouyan Esmaeilzadeh
articles.abstract: Purpose The global eldercare crisis, driven by population aging and caregiver shortages, has accelerated interest in care companion robots. However, their integration into care settings depends partly on whether older adults are willing to trust unfamiliar robotic agents. Existing research has examined robot design, functionality and cultural acceptance, but has not fully integrated mind attribution and perceived relational alignment in explaining prospective trust and adoption intentions. This study therefore applies relational demography theory (RDT) as its primary framework, complemented by the computers are social actors (CASA) paradigm and self-congruence theory, to examine how perceived mind attribution, caregiving fit, and pre-existing attitudes are associated with anticipated trust in a care robot. Design/methodology/approach Using a cross-sectional, video-based survey, the study collected data from 260 USA adults aged 55 and older who evaluated Pepper in a standardized caregiving scenario. Participants viewed informational demonstrations that approximated an initial, observational encounter and then completed measures of seven constructs. The hypothesized model was tested using covariance-based structural equation modeling in AMOS 26.0, with three item parcels per construct (21 composite indicators). Findings Perceived mind attribution (β∧ = 0.39), caregiving fit (β∧ = 0.37) and general attitudes toward robots (β∧ = 0.31) were positively associated with anticipated pre-interaction trust. That trust was associated with long-term adoption intentions through two significant indirect pathways: perceived improvement in well-being (β∧ = 0.27) and preference for robotic over human caregivers (β∧ = 0.25). The model accounted for 61% of the variance in adoption intentions. Originality/value This study provides preliminary empirical support for applying selected RDT similarity mechanisms to prospective human-robot evaluation in eldercare and integrates mind attribution and pre-interaction trust into that framework. Because participants evaluated one robot through video-based exposure without direct interaction, the trust construct captures anticipated, pre-interaction trust rather than interaction-based swift trust. Accordingly, the contribution is bounded to prospective evaluations of a specific robot stimulus and should not be interpreted as validating RDT or swift-trust mechanisms across interactive human-robot settings. Within this boundary, the model clarifies how mind attribution, caregiving fit and pre-existing attitudes are associated with adoption intentions through well-being and comparative-preference pathways.

articles.title: How virtual learning communities evolve towards social learning: insights from 204 massive open online courses
articles.authors: Ge Mu, Jie Xiong, Jie Yan, Lu Xu
articles.abstract: Purpose Virtual learning communities (VLCs) are central to large-scale online education. Their interaction patterns affect the quality of social learning, learner engagement and the sustainability of online courses. Most previous studies take a static perspective, showing only snapshots of VLC structures and ignoring how interactions change over time. This study provides a holistic view of VLCs in massive open online courses (MOOCs), focusing on their dynamic evolution and the conditions that make them more supportive of social learning. Design/methodology/approach Guided by social learning theory, we conduct a fine-grained analysis of 204 VLCs and 4,385 sequential networks from MOOC forums. Findings Our social network analysis first identifies the main structural characteristics of MOOC forum networks, then categorizes them into eight distinct types using three key quantitative indicators and finally maps out the potential evolutionary paths these communities follow as they transition between adjacent structural categories (changing one indicator) or across multiple categories (changing two or more indicators over time). Many MOOC communities show low centralization, a high proportion of isolates and low connection density. These patterns are not conducive to social learning. However, certain paths enable their transformation into structures better suited for it. Originality/value To the best of our knowledge, this study is among the first to systematically classify VLC network structures in MOOCs and examine their temporal evolution using sequential network analysis. It shows how communities shift between configurations and identifies the pathways that lead towards more effective social learning.

The impact of traceability information on consumer purchase behavior in e-commerce platforms
articles.authors: Mingqian Li, Rong Du, Andrew Burton-Jones, Jianing Xie
articles.abstract: Purpose Grounded in signaling theory, this study examines whether traceability information displaces or complements incumbent quality cues and contrasts the relative efficacy of blockchain-enabled traceability technologies with traditional systems. Design/methodology/approach This study analyzes 18 months of product-level sales data from a global e-commerce platform using a staggered difference-in-differences design with robustness checks. We apply latent Dirichlet allocation topic modeling to consumer reviews and use a synthetic difference-in-differences approach to examine shifts in consumer attention after traceability implementation. Findings Traceability information increases product sales, particularly for lower-reputation brands and diminishes the effect of electronic word-of-mouth, suggesting that diagnostic quality signals matter more than social information signals. Although blockchain-enabled traceability should enhance signal credibility, its observed impact falls short of expectations. Research limitations/implications The sample is limited to the automotive engine oil context in China. Future research should examine other categories and national contexts. Practical implications Platform managers and emerging brands can deploy low-cost traceability labels to boost demand. Blockchain solutions may require consumer education to justify higher implementation costs. Social implications Augmenting supply-chain transparency and product traceability curbs counterfeit and substandard goods, improves consumer welfare, and supports regulatory and sustainability objectives. Originality/value This study systematically assesses the substitutive and complementary roles of traceability signals in a multi-cue setting, tempers optimism about blockchain-enabled traceability and extends research on digital supply-chain transparency and signaling theory.

articles.title: How employees' AI use contributes to digital-enabled innovative performance
articles.authors: Liang Ma, Zhihao Qi, Xin Zhang, Feifei Hao
articles.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine the relationship between employees' use of artificial intelligence (AI) for work and digital-enabled innovative performance (DEIP) from the perspective of employee engagement and trust in AI. Based on these perspectives, this study identifies specific solutions for achieving high levels of DEIP. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on job demands-resources (JD-R) theory and analyzing data from 431 employees, this paper proposes a research model to investigate how employee AI use affects employees' DEIP through partial least squares structural equation modeling and highlights the configurations of causal conditions associated with DEIP through fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). Findings The results show that AI use for work exerts the strongest positive impact on employees' behavioral engagement, followed by emotional and cognitive engagement. Employee engagement (three types mention before) play a partial mediating role between work-related AI and DEIP. Furthermore, both human-like and functionality trust in AI positively moderate the relationship between work-related AI and behavioral engagement. Finally, a total of four solutions leads to a high level of DEIP. Practical implications Organizations should enhance employees' engagement and trust in AI through training and supportive implementation strategies. Managers should adopt context-sensitive approaches that align AI use, engagement and trust to improve DEIP. Originality/value Firstly, this study enriches the literature on DEIP and JD-R theory by exploring the AI-performance link via employee engagement. Secondly, this paper supplements work-related AI literature by clarifying AI trust's boundary conditions. Thirdly, this paper contributes to the performance literature by identifying key solutions for DEIP from a configuration perspective.

articles.title: Foreign Advantage, Regional Stigma? A Multivariate Analysis of Selected Dutch Regional and Foreign-Accented Speakers in Hiring Evaluations
articles.authors: Emma Bastiaansen, Frank Van Meurs, Berna Hendriks
articles.abstract: Although many studies have shown accent bias in hiring contexts, the mechanisms underlying different types of accent bias remain underexplored. This study investigated how accent type (operationalized through selected foreign and regional accents) and accent strength (slight vs. strong) jointly influence social evaluations of speakers. In a verbal guise experiment, Dutch participants ( N = 458) rated job applicants speaking Dutch with slight or strong foreign (French or German) or regional (Limburgish or Twents) accents, or Standard Dutch (control), on processing fluency, inferred motive, social categorization, attitudinal evaluations (competence, status, likeability, dynamism) and hirability. Results revealed less favourable evaluations of the selected strongly regionally accented speakers than the selected strongly foreign-accented speakers across inferred motive, social categorization, dynamism, status and hirability. The selected foreign-accented speakers received similar ratings to standard-accented speakers. These findings underscore the importance of examining accent type and strength and adopting a multivariate approach to capture their complex interplay.

content.journal_full: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships

articles.title: Understanding the Relationship Between Family Communication Patterns and Communicative Resilience Through Homesickness
articles.authors: Andrew M. Ledbetter, Kristina M. Scharp, Cimmiaron F. Alvarez
articles.abstract: We report results of an empirical study that used family communication patterns (FCPs) theory and the communication theory of resilience (CTR) to examine the experience of, and responses to, homesickness. Specifically, we tested the extent to which conversation and conformity orientations predicted resilience responses, both linearly and curvilinearly, as well as whether homesickness mediated the association between FCPs and resilience. Data were collected from a racially diverse sample of 321 participants across two universities. Results supported the mediation model, finding that homesickness is associated with diminished resilience responses of adapting, reframing, and using identity anchors. Regarding FCPs, homesickness was notably low, and resilience responses notably high, when participants reported heightened conversation orientation along with a moderate level of conformity orientation. We consider whether this might serve as evidence of a fifth family type not yet identified in FCPs theorizing.

articles.title: Origen’s Castration: Between Spirituality, Agape and Non-Binary Intimacy
articles.abstract: The aim of this manuscript is to analyse the intersection of intimacy – agape – spirituality in light of Origen’s biography, one of the greatest minds of the ancient Christian world, whose beliefs and works secured his lasting place in Western culture. Origen is known not only as the author of the theory of apocatastasis (the belief in the final salvation of all people, including even the greatest sinners as well as demons and the Devil) but also as the author of the original view of intimacy exceeding traditional model of gender and sexuality. At the age of 20, he castrated himself for religious reasons and in later years, he created a vision of ideal relationships based on a specific understanding of spiritual love, pushing genital sexuality beyond the margins of his personal and social life. In this regard, Origen presented one of the most radical and significant visions of agape, which to this day has a profound influence on the perception of the human body and sexuality. The article demonstrates that Origen’s experience reveals, hidden in the cliché of religious concepts, a search for a solution to a universal human problem: the need to go beyond the definition of love/intimacy understood in bodily-sensual and primarily binary terms. The first part of the manuscript presents Origen’s biography and his vision intimacy, agape and spirituality. The second part analyses the problematic aspects of such an understanding of love, which on the one hand can lead to the spiritualisation of intimacy and sexuality, and on the other, paradoxically, to the eroticisation of spirituality. The conclusions of the proposed study seem to be essential for a better understanding of the subtle dimensions of our sexual activity. They may also prove helpful in therapeutic practice where spirituality collides with the realm of sexual activity.

articles.title: The Way We Were(n’t): Insecurity Bias in Memories of Adult Attachment Relationships
articles.authors: Maggie C. Palmiero, R. Chris Fraley
articles.abstract: When people think about their former romantic relationships, they often recall themselves as having been insecure in those relationships. It is possible that those former relationships were, in fact, insecure. But it is also possible that people have a bias to see former relationships in a way that is more insecure than might be warranted. To evaluate these possibilities, in Study 1 we first demonstrated that people do, in fact, consider themselves more insecure in former versus current relationships. In Study 2 we analyzed prospective data from people who eventually would experience a breakup but had not yet. We found that their relationships were more insecure than relationships that did not end, suggesting that part of the difference is due to differences in insecurity while relationships were ongoing. In Study 3, we found that retrospective reports of former relationships were higher in attachment avoidance than should be expected based on prospective data on insecurity. Taken together, these findings suggest that people likely have a bias to see their former relationships as more avoidant than is warranted.

articles.title: Loving Through Pain and Devotion: A Psychobiographical Study of Love in the Life of Müslüm Gürses
articles.abstract: This study examines the evolution of love and relational attachment in the life of Müslüm Gürses (1953–2013), a seminal figure in Turkish popular culture whose biography offers a profound lens into the intersection of personal trauma and devotion. Grounded exclusively in Object Relations Theory, the research explores how Gürses’ early experiences of fragmented primary relationships and maternal/paternal loss shaped his subsequent psychological conceptualization of love, both in his private life and his public persona as “Müslüm Baba” (Father Müslüm). Adopting a qualitative psychobiographical design, the study utilizes a comprehensive analysis of biographical materials and developmental milestones, supplemented by the thematic analysis of his core song lyrics. The findings reveal that love in Gürses’ life operated not merely as a romantic pursuit but as a “reparative” and “compensatory” mechanism driven by object-seeking. Through this psychic lens, the analysis demonstrates how Gürses functioned as a stable, containing object for his audience, transforming personal relational trauma into a collective, devotion-based love characterized by mutual emotional containment. By focusing strictly on the psychobiographical development of love amid adversity, this study illustrates how an individual’s internal object world can bridge personal trauma and universal devotion, offering distinct insights into the dynamics of love and personality within specific cultural contexts.

articles.title: Loving Rodin – Tristes Amours? A Comparative Psychobiography of Camille Rosalie Claudel and Gwendolen Mary John
articles.abstract: Camille Rosalie Claudel (1864–1940) was an icon of French sculpting in the 19th and 20th century, while Gwendolen Mary John (1876–1939) was a famous Welsh artist who worked in France for most of her life. Claudel’s and John’s lives were strongly influenced by their brothers, who were both more famous during their lifetime than their artist sisters, and by their troubled love affairs with their mentor and lover, Auguste Rodin, the world-famous French sculptor. Both female artists expressed their inner life and their search for meaning and love in their artworks. Their love for Rodin sparked both creativity and self-destruction. The article explores and compares their love for Rodin in terms drawn from the work of Murray Bowen (1978), especially differentiation of self and relationship triangles. The psychobiographical approach adopted here is anchored to a hermeneutic–interpretivist research paradigm and is comparative in nature. The love of the two female artists is presented in the context of late 19th and early 20th century French life and art through the specifically described theoretical lens. Following the research findings, suggestions for further research are made.

articles.title: Young Adult Siblings’ Management of Parental Differential Treatment: An Integrative Framework of Uncertainty and Attachment
articles.abstract: Drawing upon uncertainty management and attachment theories, this study examines how young adult siblings manage parental differential treatment (PDT) through avoidance or information seeking, and how these communication strategies are shaped by situational factors of fairness appraisals and emotional responses as well as by the relational schema of parent-child attachment. Using quantitative survey data and open-ended written accounts from 405 young adults who recalled an episode of differential parental support between themselves and their target siblings, we identified four distinct communication strategies: adaptive avoidance, fearful avoidance, self-initiated information seeking, and parent-initiated information seeking. Multinomial logistic regression results suggested that fairness appraisals predicted the likelihood of different emotional responses (i.e., positive, negative, or neutral/mixed emotions). Testing both situational and relational schema predictors, results further indicated that lower levels of fairness appraisals, negative emotions, and less parental attachment were generally associated with increased odds of young adult siblings’ using fearful avoidance strategy and decreased odds of their using adaptive avoidance or parent-initiated information seeking strategies. Implications for fostering children’s effective cognitive, emotional, and behavioral responses in managing PDT are discussed.

articles.title: The Hollowing Out of Nonprofit News: An Ethnographic Investigation into the Implications of Exploited News Workers
articles.abstract: This work examines the practices of news workers within the unique funding structures of nonprofit news organizations using qualitative interviews and ethnographic methods. From a political economy perspective, my findings show that organizational concerns are prioritized over journalism by news workers in nonprofit news contexts. I argue this exploits public-service oriented journalists to do unpaid labor. I suggest that dependence on external funders reduces the power of nonprofit news organizations to do journalism.

articles.title: The Somatechnic Hermeneutic: “Embodying” the Worlds of Journalism Study
The Emerging Practices of Watchdog Science Journalists in Ibero-America
articles.abstract: Watchdog science journalism (WSJ)—investigative journalism whose objects are scientists and scientific institutions—is an important way of complying with the public service commitment of journalism. It is also one of the instruments to uphold the integrity and independence of scientific research in the face of misconduct, corporate and political interference, ideological manipulation, and scientific misinformation. But science journalists often find themselves in a “too close for comfort” relationship with scientists, which can compromise their critical stance. This problem is even harder in Ibero-America, a cultural region encompassing Spain, Portugal, and Latin American countries. Here, investigative journalism has historically been less prevalent, and science journalism consolidated later. But recent outstanding journalistic work suggests the emergence of a vibrant investigative science journalism scene in the region. In this study, we explore this development by interviewing 15 journalists from Ibero-America who have carried out outstanding WSJ on science, health, and technology. Based on their answers, we identify practices, values, impacts, barriers, and facilitators of WSJ in the region. We also identify what they perceive as constraints specific to Ibero-America, including political interference, lack of transparency, disabling newsroom culture, precarious funding, problematic relations with scientists, misuse of results, and job and psychological instability. For each of these challenges, we also identify enabling actions that are fostering or could foster WSJ in the region. Our work signals a departure from historical trends and ingrained practices, calling for a reconsideration of the contribution of Ibero-America to global science journalism.

articles.title: Political Scandals in Germany (2001–2023): A Systematic Approach to Building a Public Dataset
articles.abstract: Political scandals are recurrent across democratic systems, yet research often focuses on isolated, high-profile cases, limiting generalizability and comparability. While some studies examine broader collections of scandals to identify generalizable patterns, they rarely make underlying data publicly available—restricting opportunities for replication, validation, and comparative studies. This article addresses these limitations by introducing an open-access dataset of political scandals and scandalization attempts involving federal-level politicians in Germany between 2001 and 2023. The dataset is based on a content analysis of newspaper coverage from four national-level outlets: <em>Die Tageszeitung</em>, <em>Der Spiegel</em>, <em>Die Zeit</em>, and <em>Die Welt</em>. An initial corpus of 31,274 documents was filtered to include those in which the full names of federal politicians co-occurred with the keywords <em>Skandal</em> (scandal) or <em>Affäre</em> (affair). Manual coding identified scandal-related content and assigned it to unique cases. Documents were annotated with metadata (e.g., outlet, publication date) and contextual variables (e.g., party affiliation, government/opposition status, gender). The final dataset contains structured data derived from 3,005 articles linked to 199 scandals and scandalization attempts, with over 10 variables per observation capturing publication metadata and political context. The dataset is accessible via an online repository and a web application for filtering and visualizing scandal cases and associated media coverage. The article discusses use cases for the dataset and describes how the approach can be applied across different political and media systems to produce comparable datasets.

articles.title: Conflicts of Interest Between Systemic and Corruptive: A Conceptual Compass for Watchdog Science Journalists
articles.authors: Cheyenne Moon Peters, Tobias Kreutzer, Holger Wormer
articles.abstract: Watchdog science journalism is essential to scrutinise the structural and financial conditions of scientific research. As a crucial part of this system, experts play a pivotal role in shaping knowledge, guiding policy, and influencing societal decisions. Their credibility is embedded in a complex web of relationships that brings about different conflicts of interest (COIs). Yet, journalists’ ability to uncover entanglements and ensure accountability is limited by often incomplete disclosure and conceptual vagueness of what exactly constitutes a COI. Using (bio-)medical research as an example, we develop a multidimensional typology of COIs, based on an extensive review of academic literature and disclosure frameworks in science, practice, and policy-making. To our knowledge, this is the most comprehensive mapping of structural, social, and material factors in a single overview to date. While not all these interdependencies are inherently problematic for a functioning research system, they still require journalists to navigate them and carefully evaluate their significance. To facilitate this, the framework also serves as both a matrix and a corrective for potential AI-based systems detecting COIs. Even though transparency and critique are central to watchdog science journalism, journalists should also be careful not to undermine public trust in science generally. Conflicts have to be evaluated carefully but without portraying science funding as inherently corrupt—thus feeding narratives of science-related populism. By foregrounding the systemic nature of COIs, this perspective supports reflection on professional norms, strategies, and principled decision-making in investigative reporting—also regarding journalism’s own entanglements with individual and third-party interests.

articles.title: Mobile AI Service Robots and Everyday Politics of Space
articles.abstract: This article examines the rise of a new generation of mobile service robots that use AI for navigation and communication in public and semipublic spaces. Reviewing the state of the field of service robots and robot scholarship, this paper is a literature-informed commentary on mobile AI service robots as mobile media and their implications for human workers and the public, shared environments, and regulation in everyday spaces. We examine how mobile AI service robots are increasingly appearing in restaurants, hotels, university campuses, and public streets as service workers, tools, and social actors, introducing new modalities of communication, and reshaping spatial relationships, labour practices and power dynamics. These developments raise critical questions about the effect of robots’ communicative acts of movement, interfacing and emotional expression on others, the organisation of labour, and their role in the privatisation and surveillance of space. Ultimately, we argue that as mobile AI becomes embedded in ordinary life and work settings, it necessitates a renewed focus on who benefits, who is displaced, and how these increasingly agentic actors are governed as they become normalised in shared and public spaces.

articles.title: Silent yet Not Deserted: Associations Between Ringer Modes, Mobile Phone Use, and Digital Stress
articles.abstract: While digital disconnection and smartphone regulation have gained scholarly attention, little is known about phone setting customizations. Currently, there is inconsistent evidence on whether modifying ringer modes reduces actual smartphone use and digital stress. Some studies suggest that a silent mode can reduce phone attentiveness, whereas others deem it ineffective or counterproductive. Drawing on self-determination theory, we explore the associations between preferred ringer mode, smartphone use (i.e., screen time and number of unlocks), and digital stress, alongside intrinsic and extrinsic motivations. We analyzed data from a quota-based survey of 386 smartphone users in Flanders (Belgium) using structural equation modeling multigroup analyses. Our study revealed few direct associations between preferred ringer mode and smartphone use or digital stress. However, our findings underscore the crucial role of motivation in choosing a ringer mode, revealing multiple significant associations among intrinsic and extrinsic motivations, phone use, and digital stress. We discuss these theoretical and empirical findings in light of self-determination theory.

articles.title: Algorithmic imaginaries: Definition and critical questions
articles.authors: Andreas Schellewald, Ellenrose Firth, Hui Lin
articles.abstract: Algorithmic systems play an increasingly central role across a variety of social domains. Over the last few years, various concepts have been developed in the interdisciplinary field of algorithm studies to understand how people make sense of these systems and interact with them – including mental models of algorithms, folk theories of algorithms, or algorithmic imaginaries. This theoretical article engages with the concept of the algorithmic imaginary in particular. It argues that the concept of the algorithmic imaginary occupies a unique position in literature, foregrounding questions of affect and emotion in human-algorithm interaction, and theorising the dynamics of sense-making about algorithms in such terms. Critically examining work that has explicitly applied and developed the concept, we synthesise the scholarship, offer an updated definition, and pose critical questions for future research, including on emergent artificial intelligence phenomena.

articles.title: Rendering the whole world blank: Precarity, totalising fear and digital scrolling
articles.abstract: This article explores the connection between structurally induced precarity and the material practice of digital scrolling in the global north. It argues in favour of an expanded definition of precarity and that precarity, as a generalised affective condition, results in a state of totalising fear (fear which relates, at once, to discrete objects as well as the world itself). In that context, this article advances the claim that scrolling can be understood as an affective attachment (of the kind outlined by Lauren Berlant), developed in response to totalising fear, and which enables the subject to suspend time and to escape from conscious experience of precarity. In establishing this conclusion, the article also explores how the form of scrolling engenders an absorbing, passive and essentially ‘blank’ experience of the world, and how the attainment of this state is an expression of a limited, precarious mode of agency.

articles.title: Care, competence, or control? The evolution of parental supervision tools on social media platforms: A cross-platform comparison
articles.authors: Amanda Cipriani, Tama Leaver, Michele Willson
articles.abstract: Interaction with social media constitutes a significant part of children’s online experiences, with the potential for both positive and negative experiences. Social media platforms provide parental “supervision tools” as a mechanism for balancing children’s autonomy with safeguards, promoting this function to parents to ensure safer digital practices for their children. This research adopts a constructivist framework to investigate the evolution and operationalisation of parental supervision across Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok. Utilising qualitative methodology, this study combines archival data from an ethnographic walkthrough conducted in 2024, simulating a child’s and parent’s account for each platform. The cross-platform comparison reveals how platforms construct parental responsibility through their discursive and interface supervision mechanisms, expressed through macro-narratives, meso-contexts, and micro-practices. In doing so, platforms shift responsibility for regulation to parents as the accountable supervisory actors, while ultimately also controlling the supervision practices of these parents through the affordances and constraints offered through supervision tools.

Sciences perceived as precise and consensual are more trusted
articles.abstract: Research focused on the United States shows that people’s trust in science varies considerably between disciplines. Existing explanations of these trust gaps stress the role of ideology: when people perceive scientists of a particular discipline to be ideologically like-minded, they tend to trust them more. Here, we report two findings: first, trust gaps between disciplines also exist in France—a representative sample of the French population (N = 1012) trusted researchers in biology and physics more than researchers studying climate science, economics, or sociology. Second, the more precise and consensual participants perceive scientific findings to be, the more they tend to trust the scientists (across and within disciplines). While these findings are correlational, they align with a non-ideological explanation of trust in science: the rational impression account. This account proposes that people can come to trust scientists by relying on basic cognitive inference processes, which tend to be generally rational.

articles.title: Measuring the crisis: Quantification-based legitimizations of public health measures and their temporal, factual, and political–social critique during the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany
articles.abstract: Quantifications played an important role during the COVID-19 pandemic, not only in providing current situational information but also in legitimizing state-imposed protective measures and restrictions. Contrary to more theoretical assumptions in the literature, however, figures or statistics were not simply accepted. This article undertakes a qualitative content analysis of user comments on Twitter (now: X) that respond to quantification-based legitimizations of state-instructed protective measures in Germany. The analysis identifies three main areas of critique: the timeliness and relevance of data, its factual accuracy, and the political implications of their use in justifying protective measures. The overlap of epistemic and normative criticism points to broader conflicts of knowledge and values, where concerns extend beyond the validity of data. The article emphasizes the importance of a reflexive approach that remains sensitive to the challenges and pitfalls of quantifications in the design of future risk and crisis communication strategies.

articles.title: Discourse competition and fragmented echoes: A computational frame analysis of climate change debate on Platform X
articles.authors: Hao Gao, Yi Zheng, Ziqing Yang
articles.abstract: Climate change communication is often framed as a contest between scientific knowledge and skepticism, but this binary overlooks fragmentation within the broader climate-concerned public. Drawing on cultural cognition theory, this study examines how competing discourse frames organize climate change debate on Twitter/X. A total of 556,470 English-language tweets posted between July 2014 and April 2024 were analyzed using Latent Dirichlet Allocation and Analysis of Topic Model Networks, supplemented with manual validation. The analysis identifies six discourse frames, dominated by Action & Responsibility, Political Process & Policy, Scientific Evidence & Impact, and Skepticism & Counter-Narrative. The findings show that skepticism consitutes a cohesive but minority discourse, while substantial fragmentation also separates scientific, activist, and policy-oriented communication. Scientific evidence remains weakly integrated into both mobilizational and institutional discourse, and grassroots activism is structurally separated from policy discussion. These patterns recast climate communication as a problem of coordination and cultural translation across “discourse islands,” rather than simply one of correcting misinformation or increasing the supply of scientific facts.

articles.title: From Storytelling to Truth-Telling: Narrative Integrity in Science Communication
articles.abstract: Science storytelling can make evidence intelligible, memorable, and culturally resonant, yet persuasive narratives may still misrepresent how scientific knowledge is produced. This commentary argues that communicators need a standard beyond narrative trust: narrative integrity. The concept evaluates whether a story preserves science’s uncertainty, multicausality, collective labor, provisional conclusions, and capacity for revision. Drawing on research on transportation, framing, anecdotal bias, and processing fluency, we explain how narrative form can outrun evidence even when individual claims are accurate. We then propose six principles for designing stories that remain engaging while representing scientific inquiry honestly, transparently, and responsibly to diverse public audiences.

articles.title: Make Campaigns Dance Again: The Trumpdance and the Memeaesthetic Logic of TikTok
articles.authors: Cristopher Cepernich, Alice Fubini, Antonio Martella
articles.abstract: TikTok’s mimesis-oriented affordances invite users to ‘perform’ politics through embodied, replicable templates. This article examines the Trumpdance – Donald Trump’s recurrent YMCA dance at campaign rallies – as a case of how offline events become a platform-native trend. Using the TikTok Research API, we collected 6799 Trumpdance-related videos posted during the final month of the 2024 U.S. presidential campaign. We extracted a stratified sample of the top 20% most-viewed videos per day and content-analyzed 1130 posts. Through Multiple Correspondence Analysis and hierarchical clustering, we identified six participation modes and modeled views and comments with negative binomial regression. Findings show that TikTok visibility concentrates on event-based remediation: clips of Trump dancing at rallies generate the highest expected views and comments, while supporter reenactments and playful appropriations circulate more narrowly. Discursive reframing and satirical remediation attract comparatively fewer views but can elicit intensive commenting, underscoring a split between algorithmic visibility and conversational engagement. We argue that ‘imitation publics’ support meaning-making and production but do not automatically translate into algorithmic visibility. Overall, the Trumpdance exemplifies what we label memeaesthetic: a communicative logic in which political performance becomes a shared aesthetic template for production and participation on TikTok.

articles.title: Negotiating the Influencer Imaginary: How Everyday Professionals Construct Legitimacy on Social Media
articles.abstract: This article examines how professionals in diverse fields create content on social media as part of their efforts to establish professional legitimacy. Existing scholarship has primarily focused on influencers and creators whose work relies financially on digital content production. Instead, we analyze the experiences of what we call everyday professionals: individuals who pursue full-time occupations while selectively adopting elements of the influencer “toolbox” to complement their practices. Drawing on 20 interviews conducted in Costa Rica, we show that performing legitimacy in the contemporary media environment requires professionals to increasingly grapple with the “influencer imaginary,” a framework that organizes ideas of subjectivity around notions of authenticity and commerciality. Our findings reveal that everyday professionals negotiate this imaginary in three interrelated ways: by engaging with the influencer identity itself, by reflecting on the motivations behind creating content, and by confronting the increased labor required for content production. This study highlights the normative weight of influencer culture across professional domains by extending the influencer imaginary beyond issues of subjectivity to encompass motivations and labor. We conclude by discussing the implications of these findings for understanding current transformations of professional legitimacy.
